problem_text: If R is a valuation ring of Krull dimension >= 2, then the formal power series ring R[[X]] is not integrally closed.
solution_text: Let R be a valuation domain with fraction field K and Krull dimension at least 2. Choose a strict chain of prime ideals 0 ⊂ p1 ⊂ p2. Pick 0 != b in p1 and a in p2 minus p1. Since R is a valuation ring, for every n > 0 one has b/a^n in R: otherwise a^n/b would lie in R, forcing a^n in p1 and hence a in p1, contradiction. In K[[X]], take the root f = Σ_{i>=1} u_i X^i with constant term 0 of the monic polynomial T^2 + aT + X. Coefficient recursion gives u1 = -a^{-1} and, inductively, u_i in a^{-2i+1}R. Thus f is not in R[[X]] because u1 is not in R, while b u_i in R for every i because b/a^{2i-1} in R; hence bf in R[[X]] and f = (bf)/b belongs to the fraction field of R[[X]]. Since f satisfies the monic equation f^2 + af + X = 0 over R[[X]], it is integral over R[[X]]. Therefore R[[X]] contains an integral-over-it element of its fraction field that is not in R[[X]], so R[[X]] is not integrally closed.
solution_summary: Use the rank >= 2 prime chain in the valuation ring to produce a,b with b/a^n in R for all n. Then construct a root f of T^2+aT+X whose coefficients have controlled a-denominators: f is integral over R[[X]], not itself in R[[X]], but bf lies in R[[X]], so f lies in the fraction field of R[[X]].
answer: R[[X]] is not integrally closed: there exists f in Frac(R[[X]]) integral over R[[X]] but not contained in R[[X]].
structure_features: negative integrally-closed statement translated into existence of an integral element outside the ring
valuation ring of Krull dimension at least 2 supplies a nontrivial chain of prime ideals
prime chain creates infinitely divisible denominator control b/a^n in R
formal power series root of a monic quadratic supplies the integral witness
key_objects: elements b in p1 and a in p2 minus p1
root f of T^2+aT+X in K[[X]]
knowledge_required: valuation domains have totally ordered prime ideals
Krull dimension >= 2 gives a strict chain 0 ⊂ p1 ⊂ p2
valuation dichotomy: for x in Frac(R), either x in R or x^{-1} in R
integrally closed means every fraction-field element integral over the ring lies in the ring
a root of a monic polynomial over a ring is integral over that ring
coefficient recursion for formal power series roots
key_insight: The dimension >= 2 hypothesis is used to create a denominator-clearing pair a,b with b/a^n in R for all n; this lets one build a monic-quadratic root f whose first coefficient is outside R but whose denominators are all killed by b, placing f in Frac(R[[X]]) and integral over R[[X]].
translation_from: direct_integral_closure_check or naive belief that valuation rings being integrally closed should make R[[X]] integrally closed
translation_to: explicit fraction-field witness construction using prime-chain denominator control and a monic formal power series equation
expected_ai_method: direct_manipulation — bare AI would likely try to use that valuation rings are integrally closed, or try to test coefficientwise integral closure of R[[X]], without seeing the need for a specially constructed fraction-field power series witness.
correct_method: counterexample construction — use a prime chain in the valuation ring to obtain a,b with b/a^n in R for all n, then construct a root f of T^2+aT+X that is integral over R[[X]], outside R[[X]], and in Frac(R[[X]]) because bf is in R[[X]].

rounds.question: First restate what it means for R[[X]] to fail to be integrally closed. What kind of element would be enough to prove the theorem?
rounds.expected_answer: It is enough to find an element f in the fraction field of R[[X]] that is integral over R[[X]] but not contained in R[[X]]. Since integrality can be shown by a monic polynomial, the goal is to construct such a witness.

rounds.question: List possible ways to exploit that R is a valuation ring of Krull dimension at least 2. Which of these can create elements with controlled divisibility or denominators?
rounds.expected_answer: Krull dimension at least 2 gives a strict chain of prime ideals. In a valuation ring, primes are totally ordered and the valuation dichotomy can convert membership/non-membership in primes into divisibility statements. This suggests choosing elements in different primes to control denominators.

rounds.question: Try the naive argument: since valuation rings are integrally closed, maybe R[[X]] is integrally closed coefficientwise. Where could this fail for a rank >= 2 valuation ring?
rounds.expected_answer: The coefficientwise intuition is insufficient because an element of the fraction field of R[[X]] can be a formal power series over the fraction field with denominators that are globally cleared by one element of R. Such an element can satisfy a monic equation even if some coefficients are not in R.

rounds.question: Use dimension >= 2 to choose primes 0⊂p1⊂p2, then choose 0≠b∈p1 and a∈p2 minus p1. Prove using the valuation dichotomy that b/a^n∈R for every n>0.
rounds.expected_answer: If b/a^n were not in R, the valuation property would give a^n/b in R. Then a^n = b(a^n/b) would lie in p1, and since p1 is prime, a would lie in p1, contradiction. Hence b/a^n lies in R for all n.

rounds.question: Construct f∈K[[X]] as the root with constant term 0 of the monic equation T^2+aT+X=0. Write f=Σu_iX^i and compute the coefficient recursion.
rounds.expected_answer: The X coefficient gives u1=-a^{-1}. For n>=2, a u_n plus a sum of products u_i u_j equals 0, so u_n is obtained by dividing products of earlier coefficients by a. Inductively u_n belongs to a^{-2n+1}R.

rounds.question: Now use b/a^n∈R. Show b u_i∈R for all i, so bf∈R[[X]] and f=(bf)/b lies in Frac(R[[X]]). Also show f∉R[[X]].
rounds.expected_answer: Since u_i∈a^{-2i+1}R and b/a^{2i-1}∈R, each b u_i lies in R, hence bf∈R[[X]]. Because b is nonzero, f=(bf)/b is in the fraction field of R[[X]]. But u1=-a^{-1} is not in R, so f is not in R[[X]].

rounds.question: Finish by combining the pieces: f satisfies a monic polynomial over R[[X]], so it is integral; f lies in Frac(R[[X]]) but not in R[[X]].
rounds.expected_answer: The equation f^2+af+X=0 is monic in f with coefficients in R[[X]], so f is integral over R[[X]]. Since f is in the fraction field but not in R[[X]], the ring R[[X]] is not integrally closed.
